Yes. Using the provided single-cell immune-cell metadata, I aggregated cells into a patient-by-immune-composition matrix and applied NMF to patient-level proportions of 51 immune subtypes.

The most useful solution was a 3-component NMF model on the subtype-composition matrix. This choice balanced lower reconstruction error than k=2 (2.150 vs 2.385) with better interpretability than higher-rank models, and the resulting clustering was perfectly stable across 10 random seeds (mean ARI 1.0). The 3 NMF-derived patient classes were:

- C1 (n=93): B-cell / plasma-cell-rich
- C2 (n=120): activated/exhausted/regulatory T-cell-rich
- C3 (n=29): myeloid / innate-rich

These classes were significantly associated with pathological response. For the 3-category response endpoint (MPR / non-MPR / pCR), the cluster association p-value was 0.0314. For a binary responder definition (MPR or pCR vs non-MPR), the association was stronger (p=0.00557):

- C1: 60/93 responders (64.5%), pCR 43.0%
- C2: 52/120 responders (43.3%), pCR 28.3%
- C3: 18/29 responders (62.1%), pCR 37.9%

Interpretation: the optimal patient classification from this dataset is a 3-class NMF solution based on tumor immune microenvironment composition. Among these classes, the T-cell exhaustion/regulatory-enriched class (C2) had the poorest pathological response profile, whereas the B-cell/plasma-cell-rich class (C1) and the myeloid/innate-rich class (C3) showed more favorable response distributions.

Important limitation: this analysis is composition-based because only cell metadata were provided; it does not prove causality or establish that the classes are independent of clinical confounders. In particular, pre-treatment stage also differed by cluster (p=0.0065).
